skill.name: whatileaked
skill.description: Scan local Claude Code, Codex and Cursor transcripts and instruction files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) for credentials that were already sent to a model provider. Use when the user asks about leaked keys, agent history hygiene, rotating credentials, or cleaning up before sharing a machine.
skill.summary: Find exposed credentials in local AI coding histories without printing the secrets.
skill.author: selan-ai

security_audit.summary: All four static findings are false positives caused by Markdown prose and masked examples, not executable Ruby or environment access. The skill still introduces real risks by installing an external package and offering an irreversible wipe operation.

remediation.issue: The fallback installs an external npm package globally before scanning sensitive local histories.
remediation.suggestion: Pin a reviewed package version, show its source and integrity information, and retain the required user approval.

remediation.issue: The wipe command irreversibly rewrites local transcript files.
remediation.suggestion: Create backups or offer a dry run, preserve the explicit request requirement, and keep manual confirmation mandatory.

content.user_title: Find Credentials Leaked in AI Coding Histories
content.value_statement: AI coding histories can retain credentials after they were shared with a model provider. This skill finds affected records while keeping reported secrets masked.
actual_capabilities: Checks whether the whatileaked command is available before scanning.
Scans supported local agent histories and instruction files for credential findings.
Reports the detection rule, project, message count, masked context, and file path.
Uses one-way fingerprints to identify credentials reused across multiple locations.
Keeps raw credential values out of displayed scan results.
Provides a separately confirmed command for wiping affected local files.
limitations: Requires the whatileaked CLI or a built repository checkout.
Cannot remove data already sent to a model provider.
May report test fixtures that require human review.
Does not replace credential revocation and rotation.

use_cases.title: Audit a developer workstation
use_cases.description: Find credentials retained in local coding-agent histories before sharing or transferring a machine.

use_cases.title: Investigate a credential exposure
use_cases.description: Identify affected projects, files, and repeated appearances during incident response.

use_cases.title: Prepare managed devices for reassignment
use_cases.description: Review agent history findings and plan credential rotation before approved cleanup.

prompt_templates.title: Run a basic scan
prompt_templates.prompt: Check whether whatileaked is available, then scan my local supported agent histories. Do not install anything without asking.
prompt_templates.scenario: A first-time user wants a read-only credential audit.

prompt_templates.title: Explain scan findings
prompt_templates.prompt: Review the whatileaked results and explain which findings appear real, which may be fixtures, and which credentials need rotation.
prompt_templates.scenario: A developer needs help interpreting masked findings.

prompt_templates.title: Build an incident response plan
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the scan results to create a prioritized rotation and cleanup plan. Group repeated fingerprints as the same credential.
prompt_templates.scenario: A security engineer is responding to exposed credentials.

prompt_templates.title: Plan controlled cleanup
prompt_templates.prompt: Review every file that the wipe operation would change. Proceed only after my explicit request and never answer its confirmation prompt automatically.
prompt_templates.scenario: An administrator needs an advanced, controlled cleanup workflow.

output_examples.input: Scan my coding-agent histories for leaked credentials.
output_examples.output: The scan found two fingerprints across three files. Rotate the likely production credential before considering local cleanup.

output_examples.input: Are these two findings the same credential?
output_examples.output: Yes. The matching fingerprint indicates one credential appeared in both locations, although the secret itself remains masked.

output_examples.input: Help me interpret a masked test-key finding.
output: The context suggests a test fixture rather than an active credential.
Confirm the source file and deployment use before dismissing it.
Rotate the credential if its status remains uncertain.

best_practices: Rotate confirmed credentials before deleting local copies.
Review masked context and repeated fingerprints before classifying findings.
Require explicit approval for installation and every destructive cleanup action.
anti_patterns: Do not treat local deletion as credential revocation.
Do not paste raw credentials into follow-up prompts or reports.
Do not automate or bypass the wipe confirmation prompt.

faq.question: Does the scan change my files?
faq.answer: No. The documented scan operation only reads files.

faq.question: Does the output reveal my credentials?
faq.answer: The skill states that results use masked context and one-way fingerprints instead of raw credential values.

faq.question: What does a matching fingerprint mean?
faq.answer: Matching fingerprints indicate that the same credential appeared in multiple locations.

faq.question: Can deleting local history recover a leaked credential?
faq.answer: No. Rotate the credential because deleting local data does not remove copies already sent to a provider.

faq.question: Why might a finding be harmless?
faq.answer: Some findings are test fixtures or known examples. Review the masked context before deciding.

faq.question: Is the wipe operation reversible?
faq.answer: No. It rewrites listed files in place and requires explicit user initiation plus typed confirmation.
